title: Morning and evening
hookLine: remember your Lord's name morning and evening, and prostrate at night (76:25–26)

lines: OUT IN THE MORNING, IN AT EVENING.
cards: Every day has two doors. The one you walk out of in the morning, keys in hand, coffee half finished. And the one you walk back through in the evening, shoes off, bag dropped, the day behind you.
It's easy to cross both without noticing, already thinking about the next thing.
Near the end of surah al-Insan, after its long picture of a garden for the grateful, the Qur'an gives the Prophet a short instruction about those two doors.

teach.b: Verse twenty-five, in Pickthall's translation: "Remember the name of thy Lord at morn and evening." The Arabic is bukratan wa asila. Bukrah is the early morning, the first hours.
Asil is late afternoon into evening, as the light goes gold. Then verse twenty-six: and part of the night, prostrate to Him, and glorify Him through a long night.

teach.h: BEGIN WITH HIS NAME, END WITH IT.
teach.b: So the day gets framed: begin with His name, end with His name, give some of the dark to prayer.
Commentators connect these times to the daily prayers: the dawn prayer, the afternoon and evening prayers, and the night prayer.
And surah al-Ahzab uses the same pairing: remember Allah often, and glorify Him morning and evening.

teach.h: THE ADHKAR OF MORNING AND EVENING.
teach.b: From these verses and many hadith grew a practice millions of Muslims keep: the adhkar of the morning and the evening. Short remembrances, said after the dawn prayer and again before or after sunset.

Phrases of praise, verses like Ayat al-Kursi and the last three surahs, and a prayer for forgiveness that a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari calls the master of all prayers for forgiveness, to be said morning and evening.
Some people say them from a small booklet; some from memory, walking to the bus. Why the two ends of the day?
Because those are the hinges. What you say as the door opens sets the tone for whatever comes through it. What you say as it closes is what you carry into sleep.
The middle of the day will be busy. The edges can be held.

how: Many Muslims recite the adhkar of the morning and evening, short remembrances, verses and prayers, after the dawn prayer and around sunset, often from a small booklet or from memory, following 76:25, 33:42 and many hadith.

games.q: your day is packed from start to finish. by 76:25, where do you put the remembrance of your Lord's name?
o: in the middle, when it's quiet.
at the two edges: morning and evening.
games.why: bukratan wa asila: at the hinges of the day, and part of the night in prayer.

practice: Choose one short line to say at both doors of tomorrow: if you pray, bismillah, or subhanallah, or alhamdulillah, said slowly; if you don't, a single breath of thanks.
Picture tomorrow's first door and say the line there, then picture its last door and say it again.

wordCard.voice: Adhkar. The morning and evening remembrances in 76:25's bukratan wa asila, short phrases of praise said at the two edges of the day. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 76:25: morning and evening. bukrah, early morning; asil, late afternoon light.
